questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Circulation of a Vector Field Over a Region Containing Holes
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/1f308d1a3ecf3bd0090e22c4f70389311db4db3ff06f7038db0cf7770a8837c7.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=5,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-2,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-9,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ are oriented clockwise and ${C}_{3}$ is oriented counterclockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/2bed1b367cd101e0e90674c619ad87da8c90744df570eeea4d9b0333ccee0de1.png)

Notice that the positive orientations of the outer curve ${C}_{1}$ and the inner curve ${C}_{3}$ are opposite those stated in the question.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-5+(-2)-(-9) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/0e86380c457bc9d37d0180057d4ce8c035055986d32254d95fab3a69254531a5.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}6y\,dx+9x\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=6y$ and $Q(x,y)=9x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=9.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(9-6)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =3\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =15\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

We have that $P(x,y)=2y$ and $Q(x,y)=4x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (6\cdot 4-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (24-4) \\  & =2\cdot 20 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/e6252037001e1a5548ede86a16b4ddde8f5aec8fd956bded55a3506f7b533dbe.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{2}⁡y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot ({4}^{4}-{2}^{4}) \\  & =-120\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking gives ∂Q/∂x−∂P/∂y=−x²−y². The formal area integral is −2π∫₂⁴r³dr=−120π, matching option a; it also equals the convergent improper boundary integral. The earlier uncertainty remains because ln(sin²y) is undefined at y=0 and y=±π on the boundary, so the ordinary line integral and standard Green's theorem hypotheses fail as stated.

$$

$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}2xy\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (2-\frac{1}{2})-(1-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =0\cdot \frac{3}{2}-0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate 
${∮}_{∂D}({x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x)\,dx+({x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y)\,dy,$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{x}^{3}{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x)\,dx+({x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-3{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (\frac{8}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3}))-(\frac{1}{4}-0)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =0\cdot 3-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy+{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}x{y}^{2}\,dx+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+{y}^{2})-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-4\le x\le 4,-3\le y\le 3}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}-({x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\,dx+(x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-{x}^{4}y-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-({x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\,dx+(x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot ({3}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{728\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/16026d4ac7deeb30c1abb3a066df23a06a544116463b364b0a1e9e0bac0608c8.png)

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
\oint\limits_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = 10, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = -8, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = 3,
$$

where $C_1$ and $C_3$ are oriented clockwise, and $C_2$ is oriented counterclockwise, calculate the value of $\displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve $C_1$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse $C_1$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves $C_2$ and $C_3$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse $C_2$ and $C_3$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/11445c083440ee2fde1864d599a8bbd68146d522c61de11b3e90dc231e6eddf1.png)

Notice that the positive orientations of the outer curve $C_1$ and the inner curve $C_2$ are opposite those stated in the question.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-10-(-8)+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095196/assets/64ba92b021de2ba2f4fc98f1ce76fa0d16b3c8b7ed9ae45237cb8772b111c8b8.png)

  

Calculate 
$\displaystyle
\oint\limits_{\partial D} (2x^3y^2-x^5) \,\mathrm{d}x + (3x^4y+y^4) \,\mathrm{d}y,$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2x^3y^2-x^5$ and $Q(x,y)= 3x^4y+y^4.$ Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 4x^3y, \qquad 
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 12x^3y.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-{x}^{5})\,dx+(3{x}^{4}y+{y}^{4})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12{x}^{3}y-4{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as $\Delta_1\setminus\Delta_2,$ where

- $\Delta_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 1, -1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- $\Delta_2 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq x \leq 0, 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{1}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{0}8{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{0}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{-2}^{1}\cdot {y}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{4}\,{|}_{-1}^{0}\cdot {y}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-16)\cdot (4-1)-(0-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =(-15)\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =-44.\end{aligned}
$$
